stem:
A transmission electron micrograph of a palisade mesophyll cell from a bean leaf shows the following structures.

- Structure J: a lens-shaped body bounded by two membranes, containing stacks of flattened membranes and a pale fluid with dark granules.
- Structure K: a single membrane surrounding a large, pale central region that occupies most of the cell.
- Structure L: narrow channels lined with membrane passing through the thick outer layer of the cell and joining it to the next cell.

A scale bar labelled 5 µm is 20 mm long. Structure J is 26 mm long on the micrograph.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify structures J, K and L.

right.content: Tonoplast around the large permanent vacuole

parts.explanation: J: double membrane with grana and stroma = chloroplast. K: single membrane around the sap vacuole = tonoplast. L: channels through the wall = plasmodesmata.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Use the scale bar.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the actual length of structure J in µm.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The dark granules in J are 70S ribosomes. Explain why they can be seen in this micrograph but not with a light microscope.

points.description: Ribosomes (about 20–25 nm) are smaller than the resolution limit of the light microscope (about 200 nm)
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so the TEM has a much higher resolution (about 0.5 nm)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The ribosomes are only about 20–25 nm across, far below the light microscope's resolution of about 200 nm. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so the TEM can resolve points about 0.5 nm apart.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: J contains 70S ribosomes and circular DNA. Suggest what this indicates about J.

points.description: J can make some of its own proteins (has its own genes and protein synthesis)
Similar to prokaryotes, suggesting J evolved from a prokaryote taken into an ancestral cell (endosymbiosis)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The chloroplast has its own DNA and ribosomes, so it can make some of its own proteins; because prokaryotes also have circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, this suggests chloroplasts evolved from prokaryotes that lived inside an ancestral eukaryotic cell.

explanation: Structures are identified by membranes and contents; the scale bar gives the magnification (×4000) and the actual length (6.5 µm); ribosomes need TEM resolution.
hints: Count the membranes around each structure.
Measure the scale bar to get the magnification.

stem:
The table compares three structures examined in a hospital laboratory in Bulawayo.

| Feature | Structure P | Structure Q | Structure R |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | 2.4 µm | 80 nm | 25 µm |
| Nucleic acid | Circular DNA in cytoplasm | RNA inside a protein coat | Linear DNA in a nucleus |
| Ribosomes | Present, small | Absent | Present, larger in cytoplasm |
| Outer layer | Peptidoglycan wall | Envelope from host membrane | Cell surface membrane only |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which structure is a prokaryote?

options.rationale: Correct: circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, small ribosomes and a peptidoglycan wall.
Q has no ribosomes and is not a cell: it is a virus.
R has a nucleus: it is a eukaryotic (animal) cell.
Neither is a prokaryote.

parts.explanation: P is a bacterium.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: The small ribosomes of P are {{blank:a}} ribosomes. The protein coat of Q is called the {{blank:b}}. The larger cytoplasmic ribosomes of R are {{blank:c}} ribosomes.

parts.explanation: Prokaryotes: 70S. Eukaryotic cytoplasm: 80S. Virus protein coat: capsid (a capsule is a bacterial slime layer).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate how many times longer P is than Q.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why an antibiotic that prevents peptidoglycan synthesis could treat an infection by P but not by Q.

points.description: P has a peptidoglycan wall, so it cannot build its wall and bursts / dies (osmotic lysis)
Q is a virus with no cell wall (or no metabolism of its own), so the antibiotic has nothing to act on

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: P is a bacterium whose wall is made of peptidoglycan; without new wall material it bursts by osmosis as it grows. Q is a virus with no wall or metabolism of its own, so the antibiotic has no target.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons why Q is not usually considered a living organism.

points.description: Not made of a cell / no cytoplasm or ribosomes
Cannot reproduce or carry out metabolism (respire, feed) outside a host cell

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Q is not a cell: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes. It cannot respire, feed or reproduce on its own; it reproduces only inside a host cell.

explanation: P is a bacterium (70S, circular DNA, peptidoglycan), Q an enveloped RNA virus, R a eukaryotic animal cell.
hints: Which structure has no nucleus but does have ribosomes?

stem: Starch extracted from cassava roots was incubated with salivary amylase at 37 °C. Samples taken after 20 minutes gave a negative iodine test and a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's test. Chromatography showed that the main product was maltose, with some short chains of glucose units.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the bond in amylose that amylase hydrolyses.
parts.explanation: Amylase hydrolyses α-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why did the samples give a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's test?

options.rationale: Correct: maltose has a free reactive carbon 1 and reduces copper(II).
Starch was no longer present (negative iodine test), and it is not a reducing sugar.
Proteins give a lilac colour with biuret, not a precipitate with Benedict's.
Non-reducing sugars give a negative Benedict's test.

parts.explanation: Maltose reduces copper(II) ions to copper(I) oxide.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: One short chain contained six glucose units. Calculate its relative molecular mass (glucose Mr 180, water Mr 18).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: How many molecules of water are needed to hydrolyse an unbranched amylose molecule of 900 glucose units completely to glucose?
parts.explanation: 900 units are joined by 899 glycosidic bonds, each needing one water molecule.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 900 units are joined by 899 glycosidic bonds, each needing one water molecule.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain how the structure of amylose makes it suitable as an energy store in cassava roots.

points.description: Coiled into a helix / compact, so much glucose is stored in a small space
Insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of cells (no osmotic uptake of water) / cannot diffuse out

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Amylose coils into a compact helix, so a lot of glucose is stored in little space, and it is insoluble, so it does not lower the water potential of the cells or diffuse out of them.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Cellulose is also a polymer of glucose, but amylase cannot hydrolyse it. Explain why.

points.description: Cellulose is made of β-glucose (amylose of α-glucose)
Joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds, with alternate units inverted / straight chains
β-1,4 bonds / cellulose not complementary to the active site of amylase, so no enzyme-substrate complex forms (enzymes are specific)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds, with alternate units inverted to give straight chains. This shape is not complementary to the active site of amylase, which is specific to the α-1,4 bonds of starch, so no enzyme-substrate complex can form.

explanation: Amylase hydrolyses α-1,4 bonds of starch to maltose (a reducing sugar); n units have n − 1 bonds; β-glucose polymers do not fit the active site of amylase.
hints: Each glycosidic bond formed releases one water molecule.

stem: Collagen from a tendon was analysed. Each collagen molecule consists of three polypeptide chains, each 1056 amino acids long, with glycine at every third position. Neighbouring molecules in a fibril are joined by covalent cross-links, and the molecules are staggered so that their ends do not line up.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of glycine residues in one polypeptide chain.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of peptide bonds in one collagen molecule.
parts.explanation: Each chain has 1055 peptide bonds; 3 × 1055 = 3165.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which bonds hold the three chains together in the triple helix?

options.rationale: Peptide bonds join amino acids within each chain.
Glycosidic bonds join sugars.
Ester bonds are found in lipids.
Correct: many hydrogen bonds between the chains.

parts.explanation: The triple helix is held by hydrogen bonds between chains.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which level of protein structure is shown by the triple helix?

options.rationale: Primary structure is the sequence.
Correct: three polypeptide chains associate.
Secondary structure is local folding of one chain.
Tertiary structure is the folding of a single chain.

parts.explanation: More than one polypeptide: quaternary structure.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain how the structure of collagen gives tendons high tensile strength.

points.description: Glycine (smallest R group) every third position lets the three chains pack tightly into a triple helix
Many hydrogen bonds hold the triple helix; covalent cross-links join neighbouring molecules
Staggered molecules / fibrils bundled into fibres, so no line of weakness and resistance to pulling

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Glycine, with the smallest R group, fits in the centre of the triple helix so the chains wind tightly, held by many hydrogen bonds. Covalent cross-links join neighbouring molecules, and the staggered arrangement means no line of weakness; fibrils are bundled into fibres that resist being pulled apart.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Haemoglobin is a globular protein. Explain why haemoglobin is soluble but collagen is not, and how solubility suits each protein's function.

points.description: Haemoglobin folds with hydrophilic R groups on the outside (hydrophobic inside), so it dissolves
Haemoglobin dissolved at high concentration in red blood cells to carry oxygen
Collagen is long, fibrous and cross-linked, so it is insoluble and stays in place / is stable in tendons

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Haemoglobin folds into a compact globule with hydrophilic R groups on its surface, so it dissolves and can be packed at high concentration into red blood cells to carry oxygen. Collagen forms long, cross-linked fibres with no such soluble surface, so it is insoluble, which keeps it stable and in place in tendons.

explanation: Count glycines and peptide bonds from the chain length; the triple helix is quaternary, held by hydrogen bonds; cross-links and staggering give strength.
hints: Each chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds.

stem:
A protease was added to a cloudy suspension of milk protein (casein) buffered at different pH values at 30 °C. The time for the mixture to become clear was recorded.

| pH | Time to clear / s |
|---|---|
| 4 | did not clear in 600 s |
| 5 | 410 |
| 6 | 180 |
| 7 | 95 |
| 8 | 70 |
| 9 | 120 |
| 10 | 350 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Process the results.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate (1000/t) at pH 8, in s⁻¹, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate at pH 6 as a percentage of the rate at pH 8, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the best estimate of the optimum pH of this protease from the data?

options.rationale: The time at pH 10 (350 s) is long: the rate is low.
The mixture did not clear at pH 4.
Correct: the shortest time (fastest rate) is at pH 8.
The rate at pH 6 is less than 40% of that at pH 8.

parts.explanation: The fastest rate (shortest time) is at pH 8.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the type of solution used to keep each pH constant.
parts.explanation: Buffer solutions resist changes in pH.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate at pH 10 is much lower than at pH 8.

points.description: Change in H⁺ / OH⁻ concentration alters the charges on R groups (in the active site)
Ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the tertiary structure are broken, so the active site changes shape
Casein no longer fits / binds less well, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form (some enzyme denatured)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At pH 10 the lower concentration of hydrogen ions changes the charges on R groups. Ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape and its charged groups no longer attract casein. Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, so the rate is lower.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** improvements that would allow the optimum pH to be found more precisely.

points.description: Test more pH values at smaller intervals around pH 8 (e.g. 7.5, 8.0, 8.5)
Repeat each pH (at least three times) and calculate means, or use a colorimeter to judge the end point

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Test pH values at 0.5 intervals between 7 and 9, and repeat each three times, using a colorimeter to judge when the mixture becomes clear.

explanation: Convert times to rates; the optimum is at the shortest time (pH 8); pH changes alter R group charges and the active site.
hints: Express the pH 6 rate as a fraction of the pH 8 rate.

stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction was measured at a low and a high substrate concentration, without inhibitor and with equal concentrations of inhibitor X or inhibitor Y.

| Substrate concentration | No inhibitor | With X | With Y |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 0.48 | 0.24 | 0.24 |
| High | 1.10 | 1.03 | 0.55 |

Rates are in µmol of product per minute.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage inhibition caused by X.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: At the low substrate concentration.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: At the high substrate concentration, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: (1.10 − 1.03) ÷ 1.10 × 100 = 6.36%. 93.6% is the activity remaining; dividing by 1.03 gives 6.80.
parts.workedSolution: 1. (1.10 − 1.03) ÷ 1.10 × 100 = 6.36%. 93.6% is the activity remaining; dividing by 1.03 gives 6.80.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which type of inhibitor is X?

options.rationale: A non-competitive inhibitor's effect is not reduced by more substrate.
An irreversible inhibitor could not be overcome by adding substrate.
Nothing in the data shows a pathway product feeding back.
Correct: its effect almost disappears at high substrate concentration.

parts.explanation: Inhibition falls from 50% to under 7% as substrate increases: competition for the active site.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which type of inhibitor is Y?

options.rationale: Its effect would decrease at high substrate concentration.
Correct: it halves the rate at both substrate concentrations.
Y reduces the rate, so it is not acting as substrate.
Y lowers the rate; an activator would raise it.

parts.explanation: Y causes 50% inhibition at both concentrations, so extra substrate does not overcome it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the effect of Y on the enzyme.

points.description: Y binds to the enzyme at a site other than the active site
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the active site
Substrate cannot bind / be converted, and because Y does not compete with substrate, adding substrate does not reduce the inhibition

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Y binds to the enzyme away from the active site and changes its tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape and substrate cannot bind or react. Because Y is not competing with the substrate, adding more substrate cannot reduce its effect.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Some reversible inhibitors are the end-products of metabolic pathways. Suggest how this benefits a cell.

points.description: When the end-product accumulates it inhibits an early enzyme, slowing the pathway
So the cell does not waste substrate / energy making more than it needs; pathway speeds up again when product is used (negative feedback)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When the end-product builds up it inhibits an enzyme early in the pathway, so the pathway slows and the cell does not waste resources making more than it needs; when the product is used up, inhibition is released and production resumes.

explanation: A competitive inhibitor's effect falls as substrate concentration rises; a non-competitive inhibitor's does not. End-product inhibition is negative feedback.
hints: Compare the percentage inhibition at low and high substrate concentration.
